source.title: Minor interpretability exploration #2: Extending superposition to different activation functions

record.tranche_reason: Reuses the original toy-model code and superposition measurement while varying activation functions and sparsity regimes.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative outcomes across activation functions and a loss range, but does not provide the underlying tables or numerical superposition values in the text. It says notebooks, graphs and tables are available at the linked Google Drive folder. Prior-work findings are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The post reruns Anthropic's toy-model superposition notebook with ReLU swapped for 26 other activation functions and sparsity swept from 0 to 0.999. It reports qualitative degree and pattern of superposition per function, which bears on V1 in a variant setting. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes that more superposition gives only marginally lower loss. Non-negative, asymmetric (and smooth) activations gave the most superposition and lowest losses. The loose loss–superposition link suggests superposition can be reduced without large performance cost. Several anomalies (sigmoid, exp, SoLU, Softplus) need more research.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original toy-model notebook and a reproduction/extension, with activation functions replaced and sparsity regimes extended.
record.method_sensitivity: Activation function and sparsity regime change the reported degree or pattern of superposition; some activation functions also failed to converge.

fits_no_version.finding: Losses fell in the 10^-4 to 10^-3 range and barely differed across functions. Beyond a threshold, superposition was only weakly tied to loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, the degree of superposition is only loosely coupled to reconstruction loss across activation functions.

record.problems: The author characterizes the exploration as small, low-stakes and without prior predictions. Numerical superposition results and uncertainty estimates are not included in the text; several findings are explicitly described as possibly artifactual, strange or in need of more research. Some activation settings failed to converge.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified results for every activation function are present in the text. Grouped statements are recorded as grouped rows where the post itself reports them together.

untested.parts: Regular geometry (antipodes, polytopes and angles), the shape of the sparsity-dependent phase transition, and feature-to-dimension ratios are not reported numerically. GELU is the only function where 'antipodes' are mentioned.
Not tested as a capacity account, although importance-related patterns are mentioned (r3, r6, r14, r15).

missing.what: CELU vs GELU: small activation differences give massive superposition differences. CELU/ELU show smaller superposition than GELU/Softplus, and SELU shows the lowest in its group.
Mish and Tanhshrink are surveyed but no result is recorded or declared as left out.

record.verdict_notes: This is an informal LessWrong post with no numbers in the text; results sit in a linked Drive folder. All verdicts rest on qualitative author statements. Importance-related patterns (sigmoid favouring unimportant features, Softplus touching all features, swish preferring less important features, Softmin importance reversal) could bear on V2's importance ordering. They are not framed as a capacity test, so they are left linked to V1 only.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not report numerical feature-to-dimension ratios or detailed geometric measures such as angles or regular geometry.
It does not test whether important features get dedicated dimensions while less important features share them.
It does not investigate alternative causes of polysemanticity.
No LLM activations or SAE features are studied.
No claim about SAE features being canonical or stable is tested.
The text does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss across activation functions in the toy-model superposition experiment.

conditions.value: 26 surveyed functions, in addition to the original ReLU

rows.value: Losses were in the 10^-4 – 10^-3 range and were not marginally different between functions.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative comparison; no per-function loss values are given.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Compared degree of superposition with loss across the activation-function experiments.
rows.measure: relationship between degree of superposition and loss
rows.value: Beyond a threshold, degree of superposition did not seem correlated with loss; more superposition reduced loss by at most one degree of magnitude.
rows.note: This is a reported relationship, not a direct test of the claim versions.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured superposition while varying activation function and sparsity.
rows.value: Both showed a very strange pattern of enormous, quick superposition for unimportant features; the author notes it may be a bug or floating-point error.
rows.note: The author flags this result as potentially artifactual.
rows.check: Superposition is present but concentrated in unimportant features. The author says it may be a bug or floating-point error, so treat it as low confidence.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured superposition for two activation functions across sparsity.
rows.value: They showed an even worse version of the strange superposition pattern reported for hard sigmoid and sigmoid.
rows.note: The post does not give separate values or further detail for the two functions.
rows.check: Same caveat as r3: the author flags the anomalous pattern as possibly artifactual.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured superposition for tanh-family functions and SELU.
rows.note: The author suggests continuity, symmetry and limited output as possible explanations.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured superposition and feature-importance pattern for Softmin.
rows.value: Softmin showed an importance-reversing effect and was described as bad.
rows.note: The text does not quantify the effect or specify the direction of the reversal.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.value: It failed to converge, likely due to instability.
rows.note: Failure to converge does not establish a superposition outcome.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured superposition and convergence for exponential activations.
rows.value: They showed strange behaviours; at low sparsities they failed to converge.
rows.note: The text does not specify the superposition pattern.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured SoLU superposition across sparsity and compared it with Softmax and ReLU.

conditions.value: SoLU, with Softmax and ReLU comparisons

rows.baseline: Softmax and ReLU comparisons; numerical values not stated
rows.value: SoLU initially had superposition comparable to Softmax and larger than ReLU; as sparsity increased, it had less superposition, though more low-level superposition.
rows.note: The author says this broadly accords with SoLU's design goal of reducing superposition.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured superposition for shrink activation functions.
rows.value: Shrinks showed lots of superposition, but of small amplitude; they produced a small amount of superposition overall.
rows.note: The author suggests this may be an artifact of near-linearity.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Compared superposition for GELU and SiLU with ReLU over time and at zero sparsity.
rows.value: GELU showed less superposition over time and was mostly a smoother ReLU; at 0 sparsity, it showed greater superposition. SiLU was described as similar.
rows.note: The post attributes the zero-sparsity result to GELU's non-monotonic dip and quadratic nature.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Compared superposition for ReLU6 and ReLU^2 with ReLU.
rows.value: Neither activation had a significant impact on ReLU's superposition.
rows.note: The author explicitly describes the impact as not significant.
rows.check: ReLU6 and ReLU^2 had no significant impact on ReLU's superposition. That means superposition appears as it does with ReLU, so for V1 the state is observed, not absent.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.value: These functions showed the most superposition among the surveyed functions.
rows.note: No per-function values or ranking within the group are given.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured how broadly Softplus superposition affected features.
rows.value: Softplus superposition reached every feature regardless of importance.
rows.note: The author calls for more research on this result.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Measured onset and feature-importance pattern of superposition for swish functions.
rows.measure: onset and feature-importance pattern of superposition
rows.value: They showed very early superposition, affected the 0 sparsity regime, and led to a preference for less important features.
rows.note: The text does not separate the results for hard swish and swish.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Compared superposition across activation functions with different degrees of hardness.
rows.value: Hardness generally reduced or slowed the development of superposition.
rows.note: The author describes this as a general trend and says it is confusing.
rows.check: This is a cross-function trend with no per-function values. It describes harder functions reducing or slowing superposition relative to softer ones.

rows.subject: toy model (activation-function variants)
rows.operation_detail: Compared superposition across activation functions over sparsity regimes.

conditions.value: non-negative, asymmetrical activation functions; examples discussed include GELU and Softplus

rows.value: The author reports that non-negative, asymmetrical activation functions gave the best superposition; smooth functions were also identified as helpful in the discussion.
rows.note: The conclusion also associates these functions with the lowest losses.
